Checked the complement before inserting, so duplicates like [3,3] work
Clear trace of [3,3] showing the map contents at each step

Did not propose any test cases of your own

sessions.title: Mock round: Product of Array Except Self (prefix/suffix, medium)
strengths: Reached prefix x suffix products after one guiding question
Correct identity values (start at 1) and loop bounds on the first try
Wrote the O(1) extra-space follow-up correctly
gaps: Proposed division although the problem forbids it: read the constraints before choosing an approach
Did not separate output space from auxiliary space until asked
Raised zero edge cases only when prompted

sessions.title: Mock round: Subarray Sum Equals K (prefix sums, hashing, medium)
strengths: Named brute force and the prefix-sum map direction on your own
Corrected the map to store counts instead of indices mid-trace
Final code correct on 300 random tests; found the all-zeros and x,-x space cases

Imprecise claims: {0:1} makes it faster, key size vs number of entries

sessions.title: Mock round: Expense sharing app (Splitwise), equal split
strengths: Asked the right scoping questions: split types, groups vs individual users, settlements
Switched money from double to BigDecimal and fixed the immutable add() bug once pointed out
Final structure is SDE-2 shaped: SplitStrategy interface, Split as data, ExpenseService, two-level BalanceSheet with signed amounts that nets debts
Working Main demo of dinner plus cab showing netted balances
gaps: Missed Expense as the core entity and its payer and total fields until prompted
Skipped the validation question (percentages not summing to 100, exact amounts not matching total)
Modeled balances as one number per user; needed several hints to reach pairwise Map<User, Map<User, BigDecimal>>
Mixed responsibilities: strategy and Expense mutated User balances before being split out
Rounding drops a paisa (100/3); did not distribute the remainder
Did not answer the percent/exact split follow-up; SplitStrategy signature cannot carry per-user shares
Took about 2.5 hours with step-by-step guidance versus a 45-50 minute round; Main was not run until the end

sessions.title: Mock round: Price-drop alerts for watched products (e-commerce)
strengths: Asked clarifying questions before designing: scope (watch specific product vs new launches) and scale
Defined the drop threshold precisely when pushed: 10% below the price at the time the user added the watch
Thought about the user's experience with flip-flopping prices and proposed a per-user notification cap
Separated internal APIs from public ones, added view and remove watchlist APIs, fixed GET to POST when challenged
Reached for Kafka to decouple seller price updates from fan-out
gaps: No capacity estimate: never computed QPS (about 600 price updates/s average, 10x in sales), storage (about 500M watch rows, ~50GB) or notification volume
Guessed latency targets (ms, 1s, 5s) instead of dividing: 5M pushes at 1k/s per worker is 5,000 worker-seconds, so the target is minutes
Wrong CAP call: put consistency first by confusing catalog price display with alerting; this system should favor availability and eventual consistency
Skipped missed and duplicate notifications three times: no idempotency key, dedupe store or at-least-once handling
Baseline price is still sent by the client; the server must look up the price at watch time
Chose DynamoDB but gave no partition key, no GSI or second table for the productId vs userId access patterns, and no plan for hot partitions
Fan-out reads all 5M watches; missed storing threshold_price as a sort key so a range query returns only the watches that match
Internal APIs pass 5M user IDs in one payload; no pagination or batched jobs
No component diagram and no notification service design (FCM/APNs rate limits, retries, DLQ, user preferences)
No debouncing or coalescing of rapid price changes per product; daily-cap state location never specified
Pacing: requirements and NFRs took about 30 of 50 minutes, so the high-level design and deep dive barely happened

sessions.title: Quick quiz: SOLID principles applied to service design
strengths: Spotted the broken principle correctly in all 5 scenarios
Found SRP responsibilities by their dependencies (mail client, S3, PDF logic)
Reached Strategy pattern with a Map<Type, Strategy> lookup for OCP
Split the fat ReportGenerator into capability interfaces on your own
Explained DIP as which way the dependency arrow points
gaps: Answers stop at the definition: say the concrete outcome first (Square area is 16, the assert fails) and then name the principle
OCP risk was vague: missed regression risk to working channels, scattered switches falling into default, merge conflicts
Could not apply DIP fix to KafkaTemplate: domain-owned OrderEventPublisher with publish(OrderPlaced), Kafka adapter in infrastructure
Missed that emailReport is delivery, not formatting (SRP inside ISP); one ReportFormatter strategy beats one interface per format
First design injected a strategy into the Order entity; entities are not Spring beans
Filler wording: 'not clean code', 'so yeah', 'which is not a good thing' instead of stating the consequence
